claims.text: Carbothermal shock synthesis provides rapid quenching of multi-element nanoparticles.
Rapid carbothermal shock synthesis kinetically traps a metastable, near-equiatomic solid-solution phase.
The kinetically trapped solid solution preserves nanoparticle structural and chemical stability during high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric operation.
The initial material consists of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles prepared by carbothermal shock for ammonia-decomposition catalysis.
Varying the synthesis cooling rate between rapid quenching and slower conventional cooling can isolate the role of kinetic trapping.
Nanoscale phase boundaries and small domain sizes minimize elemental segregation.
Rapid quenching suppresses thermally activated diffusion and phase separation by kinetically trapping a metastable solid solution.
Slower cooling permits elemental reordering and segregation into more thermodynamically favored phases.
Elemental reordering and segregation caused by slower cooling compromise nanoparticle stability.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain a more uniform near-equiatomic composition and undergo less phase separation during high-temperature service than slowly cooled samples.
Improved compositional and phase stability will enhance catalytic performance relative to conventionally cooled samples.
Improved compositional and phase stability will enhance thermoelectric performance relative to conventionally cooled samples.
Conventionally produced or slowly cooled nanoparticles are more susceptible to compositional segregation and phase instability under comparable high-temperature conditions.
Kinetic trapping should remain effective only when constituent-element diffusion barriers are sufficiently high relative to the service temperature and duration.
The validity of the mechanism may depend on alloy composition and service environment.
The individual elemental diffusion kinetics and critical cooling rates required for kinetic trapping are quantitatively uncertain.
